I track several habits
- sleep, running, github pushes, mastodon tweets

Most interesting stat - time between habit. Some habits are Gamma distribution shaped, which is generated by the product of several random variables, i.e. several things have to line up for the habit to happen. The raw data doesn't say what those hidden variables are.

parts.contentText: The other pattern is habit data can have really high autocorrelations, where if you're doing your habit it is because you did it yesterday and if you are not doing your habit, you are highly unlikely to start,

parts.contentHtml: e.g. a Hawkes Process, where there is a baseline probability you'll do the thing, the probability goes up with the sum of how often you did it recently and a decay function where the impact of recent past dissipates, e.g. reading habits, if you were reading yesterday, you'll probably keep reading the book and then the novelty wears off and you go back to your baseline probability of reading.

- account/content discovery. I want to see random stuff

For example in youtube, you only get the crappy content with sponsors in the feed. You have to click, see all videos, most popular to see the best content the creator did before they got famous and quit their day job.

records.contentHtml:
Async gitlab jobs, do we have to hack support for them ourselves?

Kick off a 1 hour CLI command that is just going to wait for 1 hour. Assume that after the 1 hour wait, something else needs to happen.

My ideas so far
- job create a pipeline schedule to poll for completion, then do the call back, call back then deletes the schedule when done.
- OR 24 hour heat beat to check for unresolved async jobs, when resolved run the callback.

Some day, yaml is going to have an `async` keyword.

- 2/3 of the perf that pymarc leaves on the table is not using orjson and lxml. That's just setting coal on fire.
- 1/3 of the perf is rust code that looks very similar to the python code

Will it be a net improvement? I don't know. Native code costs more to compile, but when it runs it is much cheaper in terms of electricity. Windows 98 machines were like little space heaters. It's complicated, but native code wrapped in python is electric efficient.

records.contentHtml: So you want your v2 python library to be v1 compatible. Mapping the API via annotations is a nightmare, few people use `__all__` rigorously as a surrogate for scope contracts, maybe the suite of unit tests against the public interface of v1 could be run against v2. In other words, every upgrade copy the test suite and then use venv tricks to see if v1 unit tests pass on v1 and v2.

Set running and head off to the coffee shop, no AI required.

MMM seems like a meditation on miscalibration. Were better languages 0.1x better? 2x better? 3x better?

People really like to call out miscalibration. (for example, people get upset about arrogance, is everyone identical or is that person evaluating themselves as 1.1x better? 2x better?)

We'd be better served by doing a Fermi Estimate and stating our confidence intervals.

If you try to give `python` (as in python.exe the cli command) a suite of subcommands that match rust or go... that means reinventing pip or creating yet another idiosyncratic multi-tool (e.g. bundling pytest and flake8 or nose and ruff, etc) or reinventing Make (a config file with a line of bash per-tool). Don't want any of that.

But python could use a nice set of subcommands for all the cli tools buried in python. It would be a discoverability tool.

Don't want any of that.
But python could use a nice set of subcommands for all the cli tools buried in python. It would be a discoverability tool.

records.contentHtml:
So on the idea of a better `python` cli command surface with better discoverability. Sort of how `go` has a better one.

stdlib has these categories of poorly surfaced/hidden tools
- dev tools (unittest, idlelib, pydoc, etc)
- esoteric decompilation, (de)serialization tools
- python implementation of shell tools (gzip, etc)

parts.contentHtml:
- packaging tools (pip, zipapp)

Some of these, just need a registered command, like pip has (`python -m pip` vs `pip` ), but conditionally registering a cli command is hard (gzip would likely clash, others wouldn't).

Some of these could be like go `python test` a sort of command invoker without Makefile.

Some of these really need a gui, think complex but used once every few years

Some of the secret commands are actually in the docs but not in the distribution, e.g. the unified diff code.

parts.contentHtml: And the final cluster of tools are essentially cross-platform tooling, ie. all the things you use in bash but aren't bash builtin. This is super hit or miss as a solution (git bash and WSL) are what people usually use. Some of the tools are big and complicated (sed, grep, etc). Simulating linux shell in python, but on non-linux machines should have been its own product and I think python went down that path accidentally (with several compression commands but other tool categories missing)

records.contentHtml:
History of sandboxed computing
- Computer to weak to run host OS
- Computer can run host OS, but not enough drive space or memory or CPU for VM/container
- Can run container, but machine now host OS lags
- Can run both, but now laptop overheats, everything broken in container and VM (mouse, video, etc) and WSL and docker fail to boot 1/3 of the time.
- You know, it is easier to put each app on a raspberry pi, which is too weak to run any OS and just runs the app

Mentally I see 2 kinds of twitter/mastodon clients

- *current data*. For a dozen API calls you get an experience. Works great if you have already found your peeps, your tags, and so on.
- *all data*. You need a large dataset to do analytics, search or anything that is computationally expensive (like an algorithmic feed that uses the full platform's data to find the good stuff, or stuff you might like, etc)

records.contentHtml:
Here is a calculation that can be done but only with a large chunk of the total dataset: reach.

- Your follower count - minus inactive accounts
- Get follower count of each retweeter - minus inactive
- Get waking hours for each account - minus everyone asleep during the time posted

And 10,0000 API calls later, you have a good proxy for reach.

- Get waking hours for each account - minus everyone asleep during the time posted
And 10,0000 API calls later, you have a good proxy for reach.

records.contentHtml:
OK. Spent way to much time thinking about this.

You can't support anonymous posting on mastodon, without, like creating a pubic API that writes to say `@Anonymous` accounts. I'd worry it would get banned as soon as a bad post got thru.

But a social media client can support multiple providers, like bsky+mastodon. So I could support a pastebin or two as a provider. So the experience would be, read public mastodon feeds, and then write to an anonymous pastebin.

records.contentHtml:
Pastbins (plural!) are very unstable websites. No single one dominates the scene, the show up and go offline constantly.

You can put a webpage into the URL by compressing it into the PATH (the part after `?` eg `example.com?<html><title>URLs are my Host</title></html>`

That makes all link shortening/bookmarking sites pastebins. If example.com has JS that expands and displays the document, then the user gets a good experience.

- off site drafts - either encrypted or not

Epiphany... some social media sites have monastic codes to follow:

- codeburg, mastodon
- but also gab, twitter, truth social

The split kind of match up to left/right, but imho, accidentally.

You can use a telephone, email, HTTP and not follow any monastic code. Twitter was like that for awhile.

That leaves github, threads as the heirs of free speech, but mostly because their leadership is oblivious, it just isn't something they're paying attention to.

parts.contentHtml:
## Pastebin/textboard-like

This does not really exist today! (AFAIK!) I'm working on changing that.

- Weak identity lasts based on session token
- Some posts can't correlate as being made by the same person as another post
- with mastodon APIs
- not federated

I can't see any servers being willing to federate with this because moderation of a pastebin or textboard is so radically different, e.g. an account ban is meaningless. Moderation is based on content and prohibiting behaviors.

- Long lived account with reputation by followers, likes, etc. (users don't destroy their reputation lightly, fear blocks and bans)
- "Verified", meaning you verified you're the same person as a person somewhere else on the internet, but no twitter style verification to see if they are the right person in the real world.

parts.contentHtml:
Thought some more about this. If your employer blocks most mastodon servers, they almost certainly block open proxies and CORS Proxies (a more limited subset of proxies).

At the moment, if you want mastodon, you can find an unblocked (there are so many) instance because federation itself is a type of proxy. You get bytes from mastodon.social via something-else.social.

But if you will only settle for the full feature set, and not the readonly, then yeah, this might not excite those people.

parts.contentHtml:
Ways to save electrons on a line of business app:
- switch from the pure python library to the native library
- add an index to the db table
- slap a memoize decorator on the slow, deterministic thing that gets called over and over
- measure it. The perf loss is in internationalization, not the big O. Or it is reading the file system over and over. Or it is initializing a module that you're not using, over and over.

Traffic is spiky (months with nothing, then boom, a lot of conversations)

So I guess there is need for an alternate view. If you could mix it with your mastodon home feed, then you'd look at it every day.

No one wants to look at githubs 2 feeds every day if 3/4 of the time they're empty.
